definition.title: Product quantization: short codes, fast distances
definition.summary: Product quantization replaces vector blocks with centroid indices, then estimates distances by adding small table lookups.

beats.caption: In this illustration, split a four-coordinate vector into two blocks.
beats.explanation: Each block occupies a lower-dimensional subspace and gets its own quantizer, which maps blocks to representative points.

beats.caption: Replace each block with its nearest centroid, a representative learned for that block.
beats.explanation: Suppose block A selects (1, 1) and block B selects (8, 8). Joining these centroids reconstructs an approximation of the original vector; the differences are quantization error.

beats.caption: Store only the centroid indices; the centroid coordinates live in shared codebooks.
beats.explanation: Here, indices 3 and 5 identify the selected centroids in separate codebooks. With 256 centroids per block, each index needs 8 bits, so this illustrative two-block code needs 16 bits, excluding shared codebook storage.

beats.caption: For each query, prepare a table of squared distances to every centroid in each block.
beats.explanation: The query stays uncompressed. This illustration shows just the two table entries selected by the example database code; the full tables can be reused across database vectors.

beats.caption: The stored indices select entries whose sum estimates the full squared distance.
beats.explanation: Squared Euclidean distance adds across coordinate blocks, giving 5 for the reconstructed vector. The true squared distance to the original (1, 2, 7, 8) is 3, so this particular estimate is too large.

beats.caption: Asymmetric distance computation compares an original query with a compressed database vector.
beats.explanation: The paper also describes symmetric computation, which quantizes both vectors. Its asymmetric method avoids introducing quantization error on the query side.

beats.caption: Keeping the query intact improves precision, but estimated distances still contain quantization error.
beats.explanation: The paper reports average underestimation for both estimators, with stronger bias for the symmetric version. An average bias does not mean every individual estimate is too small.

takeaways: A product-quantized code stores one centroid index per coordinate block.
Distance estimation adds query-to-centroid squared distances selected by those indices.
Compression saves storage and computation while introducing approximation error.
